paras: The 1881 Louisville freight platform strike was a wage strike by platform hands at the Louisville & Nashville Railroad freight depot in Louisville, Kentucky, in April 1881, during which the strikers ordered that the "colored laborers" hired in their places be told they would not be allowed to work. No violence was reported, and the strike ended within four days after other roads raised wages and the L&N found enough replacement men.

The strike came amid a wave of walkouts that spring, reported alongside street-car, carpenters' and gas workers' strikes in Cincinnati, Chicago and New York. Late on a Saturday afternoon, April 16, the L&N's freight platform employees struck for an increase from $1.10 to $1.50 a day.

The next day the strikers held a meeting and named a committee to visit the city's other freight depots early the following morning to invite their hands to join. According to a Louisville dispatch, the meeting also ordered that the colored laborers "temporarily employed in the places of the strikers" be notified that they would not be allowed to work, and "trouble is apprehended."

By April 19 the strike had spread to the day hands of the Ohio & Mississippi road, and the strikers, said to be backed by a union, were working for a general strike of platform hands. At the J. M. & I. road, freight agent Hubbell kept his men at work by promising to match any other road's pay. The L&N, meanwhile, had found a "fair supply" of green hands and had 60 men at work against its usual 75 to 100.

On April 18 a group of Black men from points along the road toward Nashville and beyond arrived in Louisville but refused to work, saying they would not have come had they known the strikers had quit. The St. Paul Daily Globe put their number at 50, while the Chicago Tribune's copy of the same dispatch printed "fifteen."

A dispatch of April 20 reported the strike over: the J. M. & I. and Short Line roads raised their platform wages to $1.25 a day, and the L&N had "secured all the men it needs." No report of violence against the colored laborers, or of arrests, appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers only through wire dispatches folded into national strike roundups, such as the Omaha Daily Bee's "THE WAGE WAR" and the Memphis Daily Appeal's "CAPITAL AND LABOR." Only the first dispatch mentioned the order against the colored laborers; the April 19 report, carried in Rock Island, St. Paul, Chicago and Memphis on April 19-20, instead noted the Black arrivals who declined to work. The Chicago Tribune closed its coverage with a mocking note that the strike had "died a natural death" after much "wind," while the Salt Lake Herald reduced it to a line about several hundred "Union" laborers.

bases: A wage strike of railroad platform hands in which the strikers resolved to bar the 'colored laborers' hired in their places from working; no violence was reported (A1, A3, A11).

The strike itself is reported in several wire dispatches (A1, A3, A4, A10, A11), but the strikers' order against the colored replacement laborers appears in only one dispatch (A1), and the later reports are the same wire copy rather than independent accounts.

accounts.gist: The L&N platform hands struck for $1.50 a day, sent a committee to the other depots, and ordered that the colored laborers hired in their places be told they would not be allowed to work; trouble was expected.

accounts.label: Louisville wire dispatch, April 19
accounts.gist: The strike spread to the O. & M. hands with union backing; the L&N had found green replacements, and a group of Black men who had come up the line refused to work once they learned of the strike.

accounts.label: Louisville wire dispatch, April 20
accounts.gist: The strike ended after other roads raised platform wages and the L&N secured all the men it needed.

framing.detail: Papers printed the Louisville dispatches inside strike roundups headed 'THE WAGE WAR', 'CAPITAL AND LABOR' and 'The Epidemic Spreading', treating the threat to the colored laborers as a detail of a wage dispute.
The Chicago Tribune's closing dispatch mocked the strike as having 'died a natural death' after 'a deal of wind' and called the public 'unsympathetic.'
